hops.afterHeading: Borrowing a map: why place coding is kind to engineers
hops.title: Why a new cochlear implant can sound like a Munchkin
hops.text: New cochlear implant users often say voices sound like Mickey Mouse, so Michael Dorman's team checked. Three adults had normal hearing in one ear and a recent implant in the other; each rated how closely altered voices in the hearing ear matched the implant. From CT scans, the team estimated that the deepest contacts sat at places tuned to about 620 to 780 hertz, well short of the cochlea's low-pitch apex. All three best matches sounded metallic and needed vowel resonances shifted up only about 75 to 200 hertz. That upshift reminded the researchers less of Mickey Mouse than of the Munchkins in The Wizard of Oz.

sources.citation: Dorman MF et al. Looking for Mickey Mouse but finding a Munchkin. J Speech Lang Hear Res 2019;62(9):3493-3499. PMID 31415186. Erratum: J Speech Lang Hear Res 2020;63(8):2827, PMID 32692594.

hops.title: Try picking up a coin in a winter mitten
hops.text: Pull on a thick winter mitten and try to pick a flat coin off a table while watching closely. You can see the coin perfectly well, yet the fingers fumble, partly because the mitten is bulky and partly because the fingertips feel so little. Bare fingertips register how slippery a surface is within about a tenth of a second and correct small slips within 60 to 80 milliseconds, keeping grip light but secure. Numbing the fingertips with local anesthetic disrupted that tuning of grip to friction. The robotic-arm user in this section hit a similar wall: touch feedback saved him time mostly by cutting time spent trying to grasp.

sources.citation: Johansson RS, Westling G. Roles of glabrous skin receptors and sensorimotor memory in automatic control of precision grip. Exp Brain Res 1984;56(3):550-564. PMID 6499981.
Flesher SN et al. A brain-computer interface that evokes tactile sensations improves robotic arm control. Science 2021;372(6544):831-836. PMID 34016775.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A hand in a chunky knitted winter mitten awkwardly trying to pick up a single copper coin from a wooden desk.
image.caption: Fingertip touch signals can start adjusting grip force to surface slipperiness about a tenth of a second after gripping.

hops.afterHeading: The second half: sending the right pattern
hops.title: Turning electric tingling into touch
hops.text: In a 2014 Cleveland study, certain pulse patterns delivered through nerve cuffs gave two amputees feelings like tapping or pressure, without the tingling that nerve stimulation can produce. Pattern matters for speed too. A Utah team linked a DEKA LUKE arm to electrodes in one amputee's arm nerves; with biomimetic feedback, the participant's mean response time was 24 percent shorter judging object size, and 44 percent shorter telling soft from hard, than with standard feedback. In a European study, hybrid biomimetic patterns felt more natural, and after one participant used one of them in a dexterity task, telescoping eased: the phantom hand seemed less shrunk up toward the forearm.

sources.citation: Tan DW et al. A neural interface provides long-term stable natural touch perception. Sci Transl Med 2014;6(257):257ra138. PMID 25298320.
George JA et al. Biomimetic sensory feedback through peripheral nerve stimulation improves dexterous use of a bionic hand. Sci Robot 2019;4(32):eaax2352. PMID 33137773.

Valle G et al. Biomimetic intraneural sensory feedback enhances sensation naturalness, tactile sensitivity, and manual dexterity in a bidirectional prosthesis. Neuron 2018;100(1):37-45. PMID 30244887.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A sleek robotic prosthetic hand gently holding a ripe strawberry next to a smooth wooden block on a sunlit kitchen counter.
image.caption: Pulse patterns modeled on natural nerve signals made artificial touch feel more natural and easier to use in small trials.
